# ECS, EKS, Fargate and ECR: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=containers-q009 -->
### Question 1

A company runs its applications on a self-managed Kubernetes cluster in its data center. The cluster runs on servers that are near the end of their life. The teams want to keep deploying with their Kubernetes manifests and kubectl. The company plans to migrate the applications to AWS with minimal code changes, and it does not want to refactor them. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an Amazon EKS cluster with managed node groups, and deploy the existing Kubernetes manifests to the cluster with kubectl.
- Rewrite the Kubernetes manifests as Amazon ECS task definitions, and run the applications as ECS services on AWS Fargate.
- Install Kubernetes on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, and deploy the existing Kubernetes manifests to that cluster.
- Install Amazon EKS Anywhere on Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC, and deploy the existing Kubernetes manifests to that cluster.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon EKS cluster with managed node groups, and deploy the existing Kubernetes manifests to the cluster with kubectl.

**Deciding phrases.** "keep deploying with their Kubernetes manifests and kubectl", "minimal code changes", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: the applications already run on Kubernetes, the teams keep their manifests and kubectl, the move needs minimal code changes, and the company does not want to refactor.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict Amazon EKS, because it runs standard Kubernetes applications without code changes and AWS manages the control plane.
4. I remove the rewrite to ECS task definitions, because the teams would lose their manifests and kubectl. I remove EKS Anywhere on EC2 instances, because EKS Anywhere is not supported on the AWS Cloud.
5. Between Amazon EKS and Kubernetes installed on EC2 instances the difference is who runs the control plane; the stem asks for the LEAST operational overhead, so the managed control plane of EKS decides it.
6. Check: an EKS cluster with managed node groups keeps the manifests and kubectl, needs no code changes, and removes the control plane work from the company. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The applications already run on standard Kubernetes, and the teams keep their manifests. Standard Kubernetes applications move to Amazon EKS [without any code modifications](../facts/eks.md#eks-faq-migrate-standard-kubernetes-without-code-changes). Amazon EKS is a [managed service](../facts/eks.md#eks-faq-managed-kubernetes-no-control-plane-to-run) that runs the control plane, so the company operates only the node groups.

**Why not.**

- "Rewrite the Kubernetes manifests as Amazon ECS task ...": Fargate removes the nodes, but the teams lose their manifests and kubectl, and every deployment needs a rewrite for Amazon ECS.
- "Install Kubernetes on Amazon EC2 instances in an ...": It works, but the company then runs the control plane itself, and Amazon EKS [automatically detects and replaces unhealthy control plane nodes](../facts/eks.md#eks-faq-control-plane-multi-az-and-self-healing).
- "Install Amazon EKS Anywhere on Amazon EC2 instances ...": Amazon EKS Anywhere is [not supported on AWS Cloud](../facts/eks-anywhere.md#eks-anywhere-faq-not-supported-on-aws-cloud), so it does not run on EC2 instances in a VPC.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the clusters must stay in the company's own data center" instead: Amazon EKS Anywhere, because its clusters [run entirely on your infrastructure](../facts/eks.md#eks-faq-anywhere-clusters-run-entirely-on-your-infrastructure).

**Takeaway.** Existing Kubernetes, no refactor, no control plane to run: Amazon EKS.

**Review.** [EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane and you choose where pods run](2-deep.md#eks-runs-the-kubernetes-control-plane-and-you-choose-where-pods-run-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company moved a monolithic application into containers that run as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate. The task definition names a task role and a task execution role. Neither role has any permissions yet. Company policy says that every component must follow the principle of least privilege. The application code in the container must read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket. Which change will allow this in the MOST secure way?

- Add the needed permissions to the task role that the task definition names, and keep the task execution role unchanged.
- Add the needed permissions to the task execution role that the task definition names, and keep the task role unchanged.
- Create an EC2 instance profile with the needed permissions, and attach the instance profile to the Fargate tasks of the service.
- Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to both the task role and the task execution role that the task definition names.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add the needed permissions to the task role that the task definition names, and keep the task execution role unchanged.

**Deciding phrases.** "The application code in the container must read objects", "least privilege", "MOST secure way"

**Why.** The application code needs AWS permissions, so the permissions go to the task role. The task role [allows your application code (running in the container)](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions) to use AWS services. The task execution role [grants the Amazon ECS container and Fargate agents](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents) their permissions instead. The change adds the S3 read and nothing else, which keeps least privilege.

**Why not.**

- "Add the needed permissions to the task execution ...": The task execution role serves the agents, and its permissions [aren't directly accessible by the containers](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents), so the application code cannot use them.
- "Create an EC2 instance profile with the needed ...": On Fargate, [EC2 instance profiles are not available](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-fargate-no-instance-profile) for the containers of a task, so there is nothing to attach.
- "Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to both the ...": It works, but it gives every component full access, and AWS advises the [minimum required permissions for the tasks to operate](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-least-privilege-per-task-definition).

**Twin.** If the stem said "The tasks must pull the container image from a private Amazon ECR repository" instead: the task execution role, because the [container agent must have permissions](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-ecs-agent-pull-permissions) for the pull.

**Takeaway.** Application code calls AWS with the task role; the agents pull images and send logs with the task execution role.

**Review.** [A task definition gives the agent one role and the application another](2-deep.md#a-task-definition-gives-the-agent-one-role-and-the-application-another-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company runs all its Kubernetes pods on Amazon EKS with AWS Fargate. The cluster is serverless today, and the teams deploy with Kubernetes manifests. A new compliance rule requires a log agent next to every application container. The company wants to keep all pods on Fargate and does not want to manage nodes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Deploy the log agent as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, so that one agent pod runs next to the application pods on every Fargate node.
- Build the log agent into the image of each application container, so that one container runs both the application and the agent.
- Add the log agent as a sidecar container to the pod specification of each application, so that every pod runs its own agent.
- Add the log agent to the Fargate profile, so that Fargate starts the agent in every pod that the profile selects.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add the log agent as a sidecar container to the pod specification of each application, so that every pod runs its own agent.

**Deciding phrases.** "keep all pods on Fargate", "a log agent next to every application container", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Fargate [runs only one Pod per node](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-pod-own-compute-boundary), and [Daemonsets aren’t supported on Fargate](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-no-daemonsets). The documented fix is to [run as a sidecar container](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-no-daemonsets) in each pod. The sidecar is a second container in the same pod, so the application images stay unchanged and every pod gets its agent.

**Why not.**

- "Deploy the log agent as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, ...": [Daemonsets aren’t supported on Fargate](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-no-daemonsets) in Amazon EKS, so the agent pods never run next to the application pods.
- "Build the log agent into the image of ...": It works, but each agent update then means a rebuild and a new test of every application image by every team.
- "Add the log agent to the Fargate profile, ...": A Fargate profile only selects pods: they are [matched using a namespace and the labels](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-profile-selects-pods), and the profile adds no containers.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the pods run on a managed node group" instead: a DaemonSet, because it makes sure that the agent [runs on every node in your cluster](../facts/eks.md#eks-daemonset-runs-on-every-node).

**Takeaway.** EKS on Fargate runs no DaemonSets: run a per-pod agent as a sidecar container.

**Review.** [EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane and you choose where pods run](2-deep.md#eks-runs-the-kubernetes-control-plane-and-you-choose-where-pods-run-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs an uploaded document processing service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. The tasks run across multiple Availability Zones. Each task writes working files that other tasks pick up later. All tasks must read and write the same set of files, and the files must be durable when Amazon ECS replaces a task. Which storage solution will meet these requirements?

- Increase the ephemeral storage of each task to the largest size that Fargate allows, and write the files to that storage.
- Attach an Amazon EBS volume to each task of the service, and write the files to the volume of that task.
- Create an Amazon EFS file system, and mount the file system as a volume in the task definition of the service.
- Define a bind mount that the containers of each task share, and write the files to that bind mount.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon EFS file system, and mount the file system as a volume in the task definition of the service.

**Deciding phrases.** "All tasks must read and write the same set of files", "durable when Amazon ECS replaces a task"

**Why.** The files need two things: sharing between tasks and durability after a task ends. On Fargate, [Amazon Elastic File System (EFS)](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-efs-for-persistent-storage) provides persistent storage. Every task that mounts the file system gets [access to the same persistent storage](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-efs-volumes-shared-persistent-across-instances), in any Availability Zone.

**Why not.**

- "Increase the ephemeral storage of each task to ...": Ephemeral storage starts at [20 GiB](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-ephemeral-storage-20-gib-erased) per task, and its data is erased when the task stops, at any size.
- "Attach an Amazon EBS volume to each task ...": EBS volumes of service tasks are [always deleted upon task termination](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-ebs-volume-service-task-deleted-on-termination), and each task gets a volume of its own.
- "Define a bind mount that the containers of ...": Fargate supports [bind mounts for ephemeral storage](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-storage-types-ebs-efs-bind): the containers of one task share them, but other tasks do not see them.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each task needs scratch space for its own temporary files" instead: ephemeral storage, because Fargate gives each workload [20 GiB](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-ephemeral-storage-20-gib-erased) of temporary storage.

**Takeaway.** Files that many tasks share and that outlive each task: Amazon EFS, not task storage.

**Review.** [Fargate gives each task its own isolated compute and no instance to manage](2-deep.md#fargate-gives-each-task-its-own-isolated-compute-and-no-instance-to-manage-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company plans to migrate its containerized applications to Amazon ECS. The applications use public base images from Docker Hub. Security rules require that the tasks pull every image from Amazon ECR. A one-time copy of the images is not enough, because the images in ECR must stay current when new versions appear in Docker Hub. Which solution will meet these requirements?

- Pull each image from Docker Hub one time, push the image to a private ECR repository, and point the task definitions at the copies.
- Create an ECR replication rule that uses Docker Hub as the source registry and the private ECR registry as the destination.
- Keep the images in Docker Hub, and give the tasks a route through a NAT gateway so that each task pulls the latest image.
- Create an ECR pull through cache rule for Docker Hub, store the Docker Hub credentials in a Secrets Manager secret, and use the cached images.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an ECR pull through cache rule for Docker Hub, store the Docker Hub credentials in a Secrets Manager secret, and use the cached images.

**Deciding phrases.** "pull every image from Amazon ECR", "must stay current when new versions appear in Docker Hub"

**Why.** A pull through cache rule lets ECR [cache repositories in an upstream registry](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-pull-through-cache-keeps-cache-current) in the private registry. ECR will [periodically reach out to the upstream registry](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-pull-through-cache-keeps-cache-current) so that the cached image stays up to date. The Secrets Manager secret holds the Docker Hub credentials that the rule signs in with. The tasks pull from ECR, and new Docker Hub versions arrive without a manual copy.

**Why not.**

- "Pull each image from Docker Hub one time, ...": After [a one-time copy of container images](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-migrate-one-time-copy-no-auto-update), newer versions in Docker Hub [are not pulled automatically](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-migrate-one-time-copy-no-auto-update).
- "Create an ECR replication rule that uses Docker ...": Replication copies images between ECR registries: [Amazon ECR supports both cross-Region and cross-account replication](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-replication-cross-region-cross-account) of a private registry, not copies from Docker Hub.
- "Keep the images in Docker Hub, and give ...": It keeps the images current, but the tasks then pull from Docker Hub, not from Amazon ECR, which breaks the security rule.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the images already sit in an ECR private registry in another Region" instead: ECR replication, because [Amazon ECR supports both cross-Region and cross-account replication](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-replication-cross-region-cross-account).

**Takeaway.** ECR images that follow an outside registry: a pull through cache rule. A one-time copy does not update.

**Review.** [Images live in a Regional ECR repository that tasks pull from](2-deep.md#images-live-in-a-regional-ecr-repository-that-tasks-pull-from-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company moved a monolithic application into containers that run as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate. The task definition names a task role and a task execution role. Neither role has any permissions yet. Company policy says that every component must follow the principle of least privilege. The tasks must pull the container image from a private Amazon ECR repository. Which change will allow this in the MOST secure way?

- Add the needed permissions to the task role that the task definition names, and keep the task execution role unchanged.
- Add the needed permissions to the task execution role that the task definition names, and keep the task role unchanged.
- Create an EC2 instance profile with the needed permissions, and attach the instance profile to the Fargate tasks of the service.
- Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to both the task role and the task execution role that the task definition names.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add the needed permissions to the task execution role that the task definition names, and keep the task role unchanged.

**Deciding phrases.** "must pull the container image from a private Amazon ECR repository", "least privilege", "MOST secure way"

**Why.** The image pull happens before the container starts, so the application code is not involved. A task on Fargate that pulls a container image from [an Amazon ECR private repository](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-execution-role-use-cases) needs the task execution role. The change adds the ECR pull permissions to that role and nothing else, which keeps least privilege.

**Why not.**

- "Add the needed permissions to the task role ...": Task role permissions [aren't accessed by the Amazon ECS container](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions) agent, and the agent is what pulls the image.
- "Create an EC2 instance profile with the needed ...": On Fargate, [EC2 instance profiles are not available](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-fargate-no-instance-profile) for the containers of a task, so there is nothing to attach.
- "Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to both the ...": It works, but it gives every component full access, and AWS advises the [minimum required permissions for the tasks to operate](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-least-privilege-per-task-definition).

**Twin.** If the stem said "The application code in the container must read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket" instead: the task role, because it [allows your application code (running in the container)](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions) to use AWS services.

**Takeaway.** The image pull belongs to the agent, so its permissions go on the task execution role, not the task role.

**Review.** [A task definition gives the agent one role and the application another](2-deep.md#a-task-definition-gives-the-agent-one-role-and-the-application-another-4-min)

</details>

### Question 7

A company stores a containerized job in Amazon ECR. The job processes recorded calls. The job starts at sporadic times, when a customer asks for a bulk export. Each run is long-running and takes 2 to 3 hours. An application already starts each run through an API call. The company does not want to manage servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Package the job as a container image for an AWS Lambda function, and raise the function timeout through a Service Quotas request.
- Launch an Amazon EC2 instance that runs all day, and start each export run on the instance with a script that the application calls.
- Run the job as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate, and have the application start one task for each export request.
- Create an Amazon EKS cluster with a managed node group, and run each export as a Kubernetes job in a pod on the nodes.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run the job as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate, and have the application start one task for each export request.

**Deciding phrases.** "sporadic times", "takes 2 to 3 hours", "does not want to manage servers", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Each run takes hours, more than the [15 minutes per invocation](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit) of Lambda, and the company wants no servers. A Fargate task fits, because Fargate suits [long-running applications, microservices, or batch processing](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-long-running-lambda-short). The task ends when the run ends, so nothing waits between sporadic runs.

**Why not.**

- "Package the job as a container image for ...": Lambda allows [15 minutes per invocation](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit) at most, and the timeout is a configuration quota: [except as noted, they can't be changed](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-config-quotas-not-changeable).
- "Launch an Amazon EC2 instance that runs all ...": It works, but the company then manages, patches and pays for an instance that waits idle between the sporadic runs.
- "Create an Amazon EKS cluster with a managed ...": It works, but with managed node groups you [must deploy and manage Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/eks.md#eks-compute-compare-who-manages-ec2-instances), and the nodes wait between the sporadic runs.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each run takes 2 to 3 minutes" instead: a Lambda function from the container image, because Lambda functions suit [short-lived, event-driven tasks](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-long-running-lambda-short).

**Takeaway.** A container job of hours with no servers to manage: an ECS task on Fargate, not Lambda.

**Review.** [Choose it or not](1-fast.md#choose-it-or-not-2-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs 20 tasks of a data processing service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. The service reads jobs from a queue and writes the results to Amazon S3. The company does not want to manage instances. The tasks process intermittent batch work and can be stopped and restarted at any time without harm. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider at the standard Fargate price, with no commitment and no other change.
- Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider, and buy a Compute Savings Plan that covers the Fargate usage of the tasks.
- Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider, and buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the instance family that Fargate uses.
- Move the tasks to the FARGATE_SPOT capacity provider at the Fargate Spot price, with no commitment and no other change.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Move the tasks to the FARGATE_SPOT capacity provider at the Fargate Spot price, with no commitment and no other change.

**Deciding phrases.** "intermittent batch work", "can be stopped and restarted at any time without harm", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The tasks can stop and restart without harm, and the work is intermittent. Fargate Spot can [run interruption tolerant Amazon ECS tasks](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-interruption-tolerant-discount) at [up to a 70 percent discount](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-spot-up-to-70-percent-discount) off the Fargate price, with no commitment. When AWS needs the capacity back, a task gets a [two-minute warning](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-two-minute-interruption-warning) and restarts later.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider ...": The standard price works, but it pays the full Fargate price for work that [can tolerate interruptions](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline) and could run at the Spot rate.
- "Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider, ...": A Compute Savings Plan works, but Savings Plans are [a better fit for steady-state workloads](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline), and intermittent work leaves the committed spend unused in idle hours.
- "Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider, ...": An EC2 Instance Savings Plan does not fit: these plans cover [a specific instance family within a Region](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility); it is Compute Savings Plans that [also cover Fargate and Lambda usage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility).

**Twin.** If the stem said "The tasks serve a steady-state load all day, every day, and must not be interrupted" instead: the Compute Savings Plan, because Savings Plans are [a better fit for steady-state workloads](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline).

**Takeaway.** Interruptible, intermittent Fargate work: FARGATE_SPOT. Steady, uninterrupted Fargate work: a Compute Savings Plan.

**Review.** [Service auto scaling changes the task count and capacity providers supply the compute](2-deep.md#service-auto-scaling-changes-the-task-count-and-capacity-providers-supply-the-compute-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate in private subnets. Stringent security rules forbid any route from these subnets to the internet, and the security team reviews every resource that the company adds to the VPC. An internal Application Load Balancer must send requests to the tasks, and the tasks must pull their container image privately from Amazon ECR. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Create interface VPC endpoints for the Amazon ECR API and the Docker registry, and create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3.
- Create the target group of the load balancer with the instance target type, and attach the target group to the ECS service.
- Turn on public IP address assignment for the tasks, so that the tasks reach Amazon ECR without a route to an internet gateway.
- Create the target group of the load balancer with the ip target type, and attach the target group to the ECS service.
- Create interface VPC endpoints for every AWS service that offers them in the Region, and create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create interface VPC endpoints for the Amazon ECR API and the Docker registry, and create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3.
- Create the target group of the load balancer with the ip target type, and attach the target group to the ECS service.

**Deciding phrases.** "forbid any route from these subnets to the internet", "pull their container image privately from Amazon ECR", "reviews every resource that the company adds to the VPC", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** For the image, Fargate tasks [require both Amazon ECR VPC endpoints](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3) and [the Amazon S3 gateway endpoint](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3), and the pull then runs [over the task's private IPv4 address](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-ecr-endpoint-uses-private-ip). For the load balancer, each task has its own network interface, so the target group uses ip targets.

- Fargate tasks [require both Amazon ECR VPC endpoints](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3) and [the Amazon S3 gateway endpoint](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3) to pull privately.
- Fargate tasks are [associated with an elastic network interface](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-target-group-ip-target-type), so the target group registers the IP address of each task.

**Why not.**

- "Create the target group of the load balancer ...": Fargate tasks are [associated with an elastic network interface](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-target-group-ip-target-type), not with an EC2 instance, so the instance target type does not fit them.
- "Turn on public IP address assignment for the ...": A task with a public IP address still needs a [route to the internet or a NAT gateway](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-public-subnet-image-pull-needs-public-ip) to pull, and the rules forbid that route.
- "Create interface VPC endpoints for every AWS service ...": It works, because the set includes the ECR and S3 endpoints, but every extra endpoint is one more resource for the security team to review and manage.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the tasks run in public subnets that route to an internet gateway" instead: public IP addresses on the tasks work for the pull, because in a public subnet [a public IP address needs to be assigned](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-public-subnet-image-pull-needs-public-ip).

**Takeaway.** Private Fargate tasks behind a load balancer: ECR and S3 endpoints for the pull, ip targets for the traffic.

**Review.** [In awsvpc mode each task gets its own network interface](2-deep.md#in-awsvpc-mode-each-task-gets-its-own-network-interface-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 10

A company runs an Amazon ECS service on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The group has sufficient instances for the day peak. At night, service auto scaling lowers the task count, but the number of instances stays the same, and most instances run few tasks. The company wants to stop paying for idle instances at night. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

- Lower the minimum task count of the service auto scaling policy, so that service auto scaling also removes the idle instances.
- Change the task placement strategy of the service to binpack on memory, so that the tasks fill as few instances as possible.
- Change the task placement strategy of the service to spread on instance ID, so that each instance runs a share of the tasks.
- Add an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling to the capacity provider strategy of the service, with a target capacity of 50 percent to keep spare instances.
- Add an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling to the capacity provider strategy of the service, with a target capacity of 100 percent.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Change the task placement strategy of the service to binpack on memory, so that the tasks fill as few instances as possible.
- Add an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling to the capacity provider strategy of the service, with a target capacity of 100 percent.

**Deciding phrases.** "the number of instances stays the same", "most instances run few tasks", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Two gaps exist. The instances do not follow the task count, so cluster auto scaling is missing: managed scaling lets Amazon ECS [manage the scaling of Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-managed-scaling-asg-capacity-provider). The tasks are spread thin, so no instance is empty: binpack [minimizes the number of container instances in use](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-placement-binpack-least-unused-cpu-memory).

- Binpack leaves [the least amount of unused CPU or memory](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-placement-binpack-least-unused-cpu-memory) on each instance, so the tasks fill fewer instances and free the rest for removal.
- Managed scaling lets Amazon ECS [manage the scaling of Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-managed-scaling-asg-capacity-provider), so the group can [terminate EC2 container instances, and then deregister them](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-reservation-above-or-below-target).

**Why not.**

- "Lower the minimum task count of the service ...": Service auto scaling can [increase or decrease the desired number](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-service-auto-scaling-application-auto-scaling) of tasks, not of instances, and the task count already drops at night.
- "Change the task placement strategy of the service ...": Spread [spreads placement across available candidates evenly](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-placement-strategy-types-binpack-random-spread), so tasks stay on every instance and no instance becomes free to remove.
- "Add an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with ...": It scales in, but a target below full use keeps [the amount of free capacity](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-target-capacity-below-100-keeps-spare-instances) as idle instances, which costs more at night.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the service runs on AWS Fargate" instead: no instance step is needed, because for Fargate [AWS manages and automatically scales the underlying capacity](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-predictive-scaling-service-level-not-compute).

**Takeaway.** Tasks drop but instances stay: add cluster auto scaling through managed scaling, and binpack the tasks.

**Review.** [Service auto scaling changes the task count and capacity providers supply the compute](2-deep.md#service-auto-scaling-changes-the-task-count-and-capacity-providers-supply-the-compute-4-min)

</details>
